definition: Oration means a formal, ceremonious public speech.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oration. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oration should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The union's founding charter is read aloud each May in a full oration, delivered from memory by whichever steward wins the honor.
Remarks are far milder than an oration — a few unpolished sentences tossed off for the moment, with none of the architecture an oration promises.
A speech stops short of an oration: it is prepared and public, but without the ceremonial build and rehearsed rhythms an oration demands.

A formal address is a prepared speech delivered with the dignity its occasion demands — graduations, inaugurations, official visits. An oration asks for even more: not just dignity but ceremony and architecture, a performance the audience is meant to feel was built. A relaxed, conversational talk is neither, however carefully it was prepared.

A declamation is a speech delivered with studied, formal force — the word points at the delivery: the projected voice, the practiced gestures, the drama. An oration names the whole ceremonious construction, occasion and all. A student can declaim a borrowed poem with force; only a built, occasion-worthy address is an oration.

Marisol Vega had three weeks to write the speech for her town's centennial.
Her draft went through nine versions.
She planned an opening that named the founders, a middle that circled through three floods and three recoveries, and an ending that returned to the founders' names.
On the night, she spoke for twenty-two minutes from the bandstand, and the crowd went quiet at exactly the places she had designed for quiet.
The newspaper called it an oration, and the word fit: not just a dignified speech, but a constructed one, shaped to its occasion.
Her grandmother's verdict was simpler.
'You gave us architecture,' she said, 'and we lived in it for twenty minutes.'
